Our results show that the traditional approximation fails to accurately represent the periodic characteristics of these resonant orbits and highlights the limitations of earlier estimates at specific points in time, such as their narrow widths. Ultimately, our new model offers a more accurate understanding of their dynamic behavior, particularly evaluating their oscillations along different dimensions of their respective orbits.

We demonstrate that modeling the interaction between light and matter using a typical tight-binding approach maintains invariance under spatial translation, regardless of whether an infinite system or finite structure composed of the infinite model is considered, notably including the representation of a single photon. Infinitesimal transformations utilize spatial translation operators, whereas finite transformations apply lattice wrapping across the Brillouin zone. First-order perturbation calculations confirm that our modeling framework accurately reproduces experimentally observed results. We infer that our tight-binding framework correctly captures light-matter interactions at the atomic level, influencing both absorption and emission processes, thus implying that emission may exhibit directional preferences.

This research introduces a novel framework designed for object recognition regardless of the specific model or category chosen. Furthermore, it develops a sophisticated pipeline for identifying and reconstructing a particular object category using semantic keypoints, which in turn enables precise detection and positioning of that object category in a scene along with its configuration. Our innovations comprise: Firstly, we establish a new dataset consisting of thousands of specific object categories in diverse settings, annotated by humans with particular focus points on each category. This dataset allows us to evaluate and refine category-specific models effectively. Secondly, we design a new method for learning a standardized method to identify objects of a certain category in images, allowing different models to be trained and optimized for various object types. This method is based on a method that learns a universal method for detecting objects in images, which can be adapted to work effectively for various object types. This method is shown to outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in multiple benchmarks. Thirdly, we introduce a novel technique for determining object positions in images in a coordinate system defined by keypoints annotated on training data. This method is shown to be more accurate than existing techniques in various settings. Finally, we present a new approach for determining the configuration of an object category in a scene, based on our previous object detection and localization results. This method is shown to be effective in various settings and is used to evaluate the accuracy of our framework in reconstructing object configurations. Our framework has demonstrated impressive results in various evaluations, including precise object detection and configuration reconstruction

This study introduces a novel approach for interval estimation using maximum likelihood estimation on samples drawn from a Cauchy distribution. Due to the non-asymptotic consistency of maximum likelihood estimation on such samples, an alternative method is employed, namely empirical Bayes estimation, to derive exact confidence intervals. These intervals can subsequently be transformed into exact square regions in Cauchy distribution parameter space. The study's findings are validated through simulations and further analyzed using data sets to illustrate the results.

A new statistical method is developed to determine the necessary sample size for basket trials by incorporating information sharing between related subsets of treatments. In these experiments, researchers conduct multiple studies simultaneously, often under one or more control conditions, to determine the effective treatments. The proposed approach considers the degrees of borrowing between subsets through random effects models, currently applicable to binary endpoints but adaptable for continuous endpoints as well. Two proposed designs enable investigators to pre-define the expected effect of treatments and evaluate them at an optimal or adaptive sample size, either adaptively or optimally. In this study, we evaluate our designs using simulated data.

High precision experiments often suffer due to uncertain and varying systems, which is typically mitigated by robust compensation techniques such as robust compensation, model preview control and similar methods. However, this research proposes an alternative approach, namely scheduled linear parameter-varying (LPV) control, that leverages existing design techniques to achieve precise motion control under uncertainty. By treating the controller as a function of a varying parameter and utilizing an LPV description, sequential loop tightening is modified for handling scheduled LPV systems. By taking into consideration both the changing scheduling parameter and the bounded rate of its change, our research expands the applicability of sequential loop tightening to a broader range of high-precision motion systems.

Deep learning models, particularly those aligned partial-to-full, have shown remarkable capabilities but are hindered by data annotation requirements that can be costly and time-consuming. Unsupervised learning has the potential to alleviate these constraints but existing methods struggle with data partitioning complexities. In response, a Reinforcement Learning based Network (PRNet) is proposed, which enables unsupervised partial-to-full alignment through a reversible process governed by the PRNet. The PRNet acts as a decoder that reconstructs complete shapes from arbitrary point cloud subsets, and its alignment policy is refined via reversality-based reinforcement learning. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the efficacy of PRNet in achieving superior alignment compared to both supervised and existing unsupervised methods.

A group G is considered R_infinity property if infinitely many distinct elements in G become equivalent after being mapped to its center. In this research, we have identified conditions under which certain nilpotent groups possess the R_infinity property, specifically focusing on generalized abelian Baumslag-Solitar groups where the Heisenberg group is a special case. Additionally, we have calculated a spectral gap for these groups based on their presentations and proved that for nilpotent groups with a central series consisting of cyclic groups, the nilpotency degree is limited to three.

Technological advancements have sparked imagination around proposing various hadron colliders, 
each with a distinct technology, if funds were readily available. 
However, determining the most cost-effective option is far from straightforward. 
In this research, we consider the specific scenario of looking for the top-quark pair 
produced in conjunction with two Higgs bosons or two bottom-quark pairs at a future collider. 
We estimate how many events would need to be collected for a future collider to match 
the data obtained from the LHC and future colliders like the HL-LHC, 
the FCC-hh, or the CLIC at 1.5 TeV. 
By using Monte Carlo simulations, we analyzed the number of events required for 
both signal and background processes at 3 sigma significance, 
then compared the performance of four possible technologies: 
high-luminosity p-p (100 TeV), e+e- (3 TeV), e+e- at center-of-mass 2.5 times the top-quark mass, 
and e-e (800 GeV). 
We discovered that a 100 TeV p-p collider, with its high luminosity, 
is the most efficient in producing data equivalent to the combined efforts of 
an electron collider operating at 3 TeV and 10 years, 
as well as CLIC at 1.5 TeV and 1.5 years. 
Our analysis also

In time-resolved spectroscopy, obtaining information about molecular dynamics from signal decay curves is becoming a crucial objective.  The application of numerical methods for analyzing transient signal patterns has garnered significant interest.  The Adjoint Sensitivity Analysis Method is an effective tool for assessing the impact of input variations on output sensitivity in complex systems.  Recent developments have enabled the use of AMSAM for determining the optimal trajectory that best fits experimental signal decay curves in molecular dynamics simulations.  This research extends these methods to determine multiple states of a dynamic system within broad trajectory ensembles across the entire simulation period.  The method demonstrates successful results in determining multiple states of water hydroxide ions at the atomic level, as well as other systems utilizing transient signal spectra.

The known internal structures of mesons are described in detail using the Bethe-Salpeter formalism. Using this, we apply the Feynman-Manashov technique to calculate the wave functions and spectral functions for the D* and D*s mesons within the light-front holographic QCD framework. Next, we analyze the wave functions at different momentum transfer levels (q2) to derive the distribution profiles (duality functions) of D* and D*s wave functions. The distribution profiles of D* and D*s are found to have distinct shapes that change with q2. The ultimate goal is to utilize these distribution profiles in conjunction with a model of light cone operator product expansion, allowing for the computation of second moments and light-ray matrix elements. This model will then be applied in evaluating correlation functions related to semi-leptonic decays involving D* and D\s mesons.

We investigate key properties of Lebesgue measurable functions based on specific for transforms within particular Gelfand-Shilov spaces, satisfying crucial inequalities that yield soft embeddings. The conditions we propose characterize these spaces and compare them to classical characterizations using growth estimates of Fourier transforms. The analyses we conduct provide embeddings of Sobolev spaces, including an application to show that a certain class of Toeplitz operators cannot map Sobolev spaces onto $L^2$. Furthermore, utilizing the characterizations, we demonstrate that for any $\sigma$ between 0 and 1, the restricted Toeplitz algebras on any non-compact symplectic manifold are not Gelfand-Shilov space valued for $\sigma$.

Instance segmentation is a well-established task in computer vision, yet it becomes significantly more difficult when dealing with novel modalities, especially if training data for these new modalities is unlabelled. To tackle this challenge in the medical field, where multiple imaging modalities are commonly used, we have developed a Cycle Division Generative Adversarial Network (CD-GAN) that can leverage unlabeled data to perform instance segmentation. CD-GAN builds upon the principles of CycleGAN by incorporating an identity loss to ensure realistic image transformations, while introducing a new modality preservation loss to retain structural information from the source domain, all aimed at enhancing the performance of the model. Notably, our model demonstrates remarkable results on the Synapse dataset for prostate cancer segmentation across four different imaging modalities.

A well-regarded approach to predicting dynamic movements involves the integration of Recurrent Neural Networks, particularly those with recurrent connections. To overcome the limitations of traditional graph nodes and edges, which are commonly used to represent motion, our research focuses on developing novel nodes and edges using Radial Basis Function kernels for both spatial and temporal dimensions, respectively. These innovative elements enable the effective capture of action features and motion dynamics. Following this, we develop an model based on a Recurrent Neural Network that is designed to excel in action classification tasks. Notably, the performance of our proposed model significantly surpasses the state-of-the-art benchmarks on three major action recognition datasets, namely Kinetics, KIT, and Subcm.

A remarkable UV continuum emission was observed during AD Leo's Great Flare on April 12 due to electron-impact excitation on Fe II atoms, as reported by Landi et al. (2015). This unusual emission has not been successfully modeled using conventional magnetic reconnection plasma models. Our investigation employed radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations with self-consistent computation of UV continuum energy levels to understand the feasibility of such plasma models producing the observed emission. Although these simulations could replicate the observed Fe II emission intensity and near-infrared continuum, they failed to match the near-ultraviolet data. This discrepancy suggests that significant additional energy input mechanisms are needed to explain the unusual near-ultraviolet energy output, beyond the electron kinetic energy released through magnetic reconnection.

We explore deformations of G2-instantons on nearly G2 manifolds with the standard G2 structure comprising of the G2 3-form. Our research reveals that in the case of nearly G2 structures derived from SU3 complex structures on almost complex surfaces, we can demonstrate that such deformations constitute a special case of more general Abelian projection deformation. Building upon this finding, we establish a correspondence between the instances where these deformations abate and instances where the associated complex structures exhibit complex structure tensors that are integrable. We then apply our results to construct instances of G2-instantons on nearly G2 geometries, specifically including of the product spaces of circles with complex surfaces. We also discuss extensions of these deformations to include Su2xU1 and Su3 reductions of the Spin(7) instantons.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be considered C-normal if there exists a conjugation $C$ such that $NT^*N = T^*N^*N = N T^*N$. In the context of function spaces, a study has been undertaken on the C-normality of composition operators and weighted composition operators with specific symbols in $H^2$, a standard space in the theory of function spaces. Furthermore, for certain classes of operators, necessary and sufficient conditions for C-normality have been established.

A number theory concept, the additive residue graph, has been explored with a focus on its properties when the graph's vertex count is a multiple of a prime number. Researchers determined the core components that can be formed from sequences of integers where each element is relatively prime to the prime number. These core components were found to be isomorphic to each other and contain specific walk patterns, which further led to a more comprehensive classification of all possible core components that can be formed when the vertex count is a high power of the prime number.

Recent techniques in point cloud denoising achieve remarkable success in removing noise, but often produce non-uniform model parameters due to excessive detail preservation, which can be detrimental in real-world applications like building CNR models from low-quality scans. Our novel approach, Transformation-Unique Smoothing, addresses these challenges by developing a novel point cloud denoising technique tailored for 3D model denoising and uniformization, with an emphasis on detail preservation. Unlike traditional methods, our technique eliminates the limitations of neighborhood-based approaches and excessive detail, achieving a balanced blend of denoising, smoothing, and detail retention through the integration of local and global features. Specifically, our method tackles transformation sensitivity and excessive detail issues by deriving feature representations that are invariant to geometric transformations and excessive details, respectively. Our technique's performance is thoroughly evaluated against state-of-the-art denoising methods through comprehensive experiments covering various real-world scenarios, demonstrating its superior capabilities in removing noise, smoothing, and preserving details.

We examine how Multi-Channel Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) networks operate using probabilistic medium access control methods. A novel probabilistic framework is developed to analyze Far-field Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) signals, which overlap in both frequency and time. This framework serves as a foundation for evaluating Far-field FMCW access methods. Our analysis reveals that Slotted ALOHA achieves a maximum system throughput of approximately 63%, whereas an enhanced variant can reach a maximum of around 95%. Additionally, we develop an analytical approach to determine the average delay of targets and find it aligns well with simulation outcomes across various network conditions. Furthermore, we analyze a Carrier Sense Multiple Access (CSMA) mechanism and create both an exact and approximate analytical model for calculating target delay, which demonstrates better performance than traditional ALOHA-based systems.

Experiments involving Hong-Ou-Mandel interference have been utilized to investigate the entwined two-photon absorption entanglement effect, where physical quantities like refractive index and wave vector are modified during a specific process. A potential concern is whether this entwined two-photon absorption process can occur simultaneously with the photon interference process. We investigated this question by applying spectral analysis to the spectral density approach in order to distinguish these processes. Our findings demonstrate that the entwined two-photon absorption process is always accompanied by the photon interference process under linear driving conditions, regardless of whether the system is in resonance or out of resonance. Nonetheless, if the driving field intensity surpasses a certain critical point called the Raman threshold, the entwined two-photon absorption process becomes decoupled from the photon interference process and exhibits characteristics similar to stimulated Raman scattering. Our analysis is based on two-photon Rabi models based on the JC model and the atomic Bose-Einstein condensation model, which further confirms that the entwined two-photon absorption process will occur alongside the photon interference process for any two-level or three-level atomic BEC system under linear driving conditions.

We establish that the local triviality of elliptic cohomology for complex vector spaces with T^n symmetry implies its application to principal C^*-bundle projections from CP(V) to Gr(V,1), allowing for the derivation of formulae in elliptic cohomology using Segal's axioms, specifically that for any such projection with fiber S, both the local behavior and the Whitney functorial property are sufficient to determine that E(S) to E(Gr(V,1))-map is explicitly expressed.

Despite advancements in KGRN, KGRMs still face challenges in efficiently representing temporal events within knowledge graphs. Many existing KGRMs rely on pre-established models, limiting their applicability. We introduce KNRG, a novel framework for KGRN that incorporates a low-rank model for dynamic temporal knowledge graph representation, enabling scalable and coherent event modeling regardless of the underlying structure. KNRG employs a graph neural network to predict evolving knowledge relationships over time. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that KNRG outperforms existing KGRN methods and provides robust predictions for rare events, particularly those with sparse temporal occurrences.

In a specific type of ground state formed in experiments with ultracold atoms and sound waves, the influence of the acoustic waves creates a series of periodic peaks in the atomic density. These dense regions, referred to as phonon-induced condensates, consist of areas where the atomic interactions are significantly influenced by the sound waves. The areas within these condensates exhibit variations in sound wave amplitude and atomic density, which have a substantial impact on the behavior of the atoms and the characteristics of the phonons. Due to these interactions, the phonons develop unique properties and unusual effects as they propagate through the condensates. This paper examines these phenomena and unusual effects in detail.

We demonstrate that it's possible to perfectly separate nonlocal outcomes in a scenario with multiple inputs and outputs, using a strategy that relies on perfect correlations rather than statistical inequalities. Although perfect correlations are rarely achieved exactly in experiments, our research confirms that these correlations are robust against minor deviations. Moreover, we examine nonlocal demonstrations relying on conditional independence rather than perfect correlations, revealing that this ideal scenario case holds significance even when demarginalization artifacts are present. Specifically, our findings indicate that nonlocality can be unequivocally established in nine-qubit and six-qutrit entangled states, similar to the WOOT experiment, yet using a strategy that's simpler and more resilient to imperfections than the original.

In search of novel solutions to the longstanding problems of achieving a stable, one-step cosmological model and understanding dark energy, researchers have turned to models featuring flat lines. A significant breakthrough occurred with the development of the CDE model, which incorporated a derivative of dark energy proportional to its first derivative of the Hubble parameter. Although initially met with challenges in a variety of contexts, including a straightforward flat line in a matter-dominated universe, some simple models have since been identified that effectively reproduce the flat line's behavior. Using a modified cosmological perturbation code, researchers were able to obtain a precise solution for perturbation evolution during the flat line phase and discover that a particular parameter determines whether dark energy becomes clustered or smooth. Based on this discovery, they calculated predictions for weak gravitational lensing effects, which in turn enabled them to constrain the space of possible modifications to cosmological constant energy density. Their analysis revealed significant limits on these modifications in lensing-dominated regions of the sky, which in turn led to novel limits on modified cosmological models.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolattice, $\beta-C_3N_4$ analog, exhibits potential as superconducting material due to its exceptional stability and boron doping-induced stability. However, theoretical analysis utilizing first-principles calculations indicates lower than expected superconducting temperatures ($T_c$) in the range of 10-20 K, likely due to weak electronic band structure and intrinsic stability resulting in $\beta-C_3N_4$-like structure. Consequently, further investigation is necessary to explore other hydrogen boride compositions which may exhibit superior superconducting properties.

The Flattened Partitions model serves as a foundational tool for analyzing runner allocation strategies in sports competitions. Through the lens of this model, we examine its properties and derive calculations for key metrics including total allocations, probability distribution of team allocation patterns, expected team participation, and variance of such expectations. The framework is exemplified through its application to real-world scenarios such as rugby and tennis tournaments. The insights derived from this analysis facilitate further research in sports analytics and the evaluation of tournament design.

Recent studies revealed that positive curvature on quaternionic manifolds implies 
the first Chern-Ricci form's positivity, meaning the associated arithmetic groups 
exhibit charmability. Recently, standard conjectures were formulated to describe 
the associated cohomology's generation, taking curvature properties into account.
We developed a new technique to determine positivity of Chern-Ricci forms by using
stochastic processes on the associated quaternionic manifold and quotient spaces.
Our approach enabled explicit computation of Chern classes up to the associated 
group's rank, particularly the second class. Moreover, we introduced a new model 
to study the associated group cohomology's growth, reflecting rank and stiffness.
This model supported numerical investigations into charmability and cohomological 
structures for a variety of quaternionic unitary group families.

Highway driving systems designed with failure protection mechanisms can be reliably validated using model checking methods. This approach was successful in formally verifying a highly complex, real-world driving system for a vehicle, which is capable of operating continuously in the event of a failure and autonomously returning it to normal function.

This research explores the dynamic changes in a system's future behavior through the lens of its underlying nonlinear dynamics. We introduce a novel approach to uncovering distinct patterns in future system trajectories by clustering them according to their impact on the system's evolution. These clusters are not pre-defined, but rather emerge from an unsupervised learning process that segments the system's state space into distinct, dynamically meaningful regions. We derive measures to quantify the difference between these regions and identify their boundaries, providing insights into their significance. We evaluate our approach using a variety of well-known nonlinear systems, demonstrating its ability to reveal novel insights into their underlying dynamics. Notably, our results in weather systems provide new interpretations of storm development, illustrating the methodology's practical applications beyond its theoretical value.

I will present three approaches to non-standard analysis - NS, C-NS, and I-NS - that are based on different understandings of Leibniz's reasoning. These approaches rely on the same fundamental concepts such as infinitesimals, monads, and hyper-reals but offer distinct perspectives on infinite numbers, reals, and ghosts, respectively. I-NS is a recent framework developed by Schiemmer, which incorporates ideas from Schroeder's reasoning in Mechanics at a formal level. Notably, Schiemmer's reasoning has historical roots in Magnus's work, which pre-dates Schrodinger's theories in Mechanics by over a century.

Using large radio telescopes like FAST and SKA, 21cm intensity mapping is emerging as a highly efficient method for studying large-scale hydrogen 21cm absorption. However, this approach faces a major challenge due to the overwhelming influence of DC electric fields in the radio spectrum. To optimize data collection and analysis, newly developed techniques such as using the sphere of influence have enhanced the efficiency of foreground removal without compromising the signal of interest. This research aims to investigate how these techniques affect data extraction from simulated data sets generated by a realistic model of the sphere of influence. The study found that foreground removal can significantly reduce data quality, potentially hindering scientific outcomes. The findings suggest that further theoretical and practical improvements are necessary to ensure accurate data interpretation and maximize the potential of large-scale hydrogen 21cm imaging.

Independent systems emerge from a natural extension of vector spaces over fields without infinitesimal elements to systems over fields with infinite elements. Operators that maintain linear relationships when added to elements of a field with infinite elements can be used to define an independence relationship among a set of functions that assign values from the extended field to elements of an original, independent system. As a result, a vector space that exists over its original field of values is equivalent to an independent system over its field with infinite elements.

Conventional recommender systems primarily depend on user-item interactions to generate recommendations, but this approach to similar items may fall short due to its narrow perspective. As a result, research has expanded to encompass multiple data sources in order to broaden its understanding. This paper builds on existing hybrid recommender systems that combine methods utilizing user data and item data to improve recommendations. Our system enhances hybrid recommender systems by integrating two techniques, utilizing context-aware document analysis and user behavior tracking, in order to enhance its capabilities and provide more accurate recommendations.

Using the sparse graph approach, we establish the openness of type B junctions and asymptotic simplicity for conditions on matrices with random entries. This achievement removes the previously necessary constraints on the variance. Applying our findings to models from quantum mechanics, we demonstrate that the associated conditional free probability is unitarily equivalent to standard free probability.

We examine the problem of detecting whether a property respecting timing can be observed in a real-time marked system, specifically focusing on properties expressible using timed automata or restricted subsets of first-order logic with timing constraints. Our proposed solution leverages discrete temporal logics and automata along with half-automata, offering an alternative approach compared to earlier submissions.

The decay process $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ is analyzed in detail. Assuming that the $a_0(980)$ resonance has the same dynamic behavior as the $f_0(980)$ resonance but does not couple to the $\pi^0\eta$ channel, the $S$-wave amplitude is decomposed into resonant and non-resonant components and subsequently fitted to $\pi^0\eta$ decay data from two experiments: LHCb and BESIII. As a result, key $f_0(980)$ resonance parameters are determined: its coupling to the $K^+K^-$ channel is $g_{K^+K^-}=12.0^{+2.1}_{-1.4}$ MeV, and its coupling to the $\pi^0\eta$ channel is $g_{\pi^0\eta}=5.0^{+1.1}_{-0.5}$ MeV. Additionally, a non-resonant term $R=4.0^{+1.0}_{-0.4}$ MeV is found, and a limit for the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980)$ branching ratio is established as ${\cal B}(\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi a_0(980))<1

The GRAVITY observing mode utilizes four 2-metre diameter telescopes within the Very Large Telescope Interferometer to adjust their relative positioning, simulating longer baselines up to 250 metres. This configuration enables precise measurements in astronomical applications like exoplanet characterization and black hole orbit determination. Our research characterizes the GRAVITY observing mode's performance by producing reference observations of stable celestial objects. These studies involve analyzing point spread functions for bright stars and resolving planetary-mass objects like WR 107 and $\mu$ Orionis. Our findings include interferometric phases and amplitudes, as well as reveal residual atmospheric effects on the GRAVITY mode, leaving approximately 10 milliarcseconds of uncertainty in phase accuracy after accounting for atmospheric turbulence.

The application of approximation algorithms to geometric problems has seen substantial advancement over recent decades. This paper focuses on the Euclidean k-Center problem, where the goal is to find a set of centers minimizing a specific cost function depending on a parameter k. We examine the efficiency with which this problem can be approximated in terms of dimensionality, demonstrating that in spaces with a certain property known as "Freeway dimension," these problems can be efficiently approximated up to a certain factor, whereas, on average, such efficiency cannot be achieved in two dimensions. This result holds for a broader class of problems. To accomplish this, we employ an approach that utilizes polynomial multiplicative preprocessing techniques to efficiently reduce the problem size before applying known approximation methods, an approach we suggest could potentially yield benefits for related problems as well.

In this study, we focus on entire functions of finite order and establish the uniqueness of such functions based on their finite exponential type or order, provided they satisfy the condition $f(\zeta + \eta) = h(\zeta)g(\eta)$ for entire functions $h$ and $g$ of order less than the original function's order, where $\eta$ represents a nonzero constant.

In the context of solving polynomial linear systems, we explore early termination techniques that leverage randomness and permit certain inaccuracies to quickly obtain approximated solutions. We first modify the classical Berlekamp-Massey-Cossey algorithm to achieve optimal results in error-prone scenarios without relying on specific error patterns. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this modified algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods in multiple test cases. Additionally, we integrate a variational approach combining matrix approximation and the Schur complement to solve an optimized subproblem under constraints. Notably, our method can prematurely exit the process by identifying when further improvements would exceed a specified tolerance level. The enhanced algorithm exhibits superior performance in both speed and accuracy when compared to competing solutions.

The continuous flow of data packages in modern network infrastructure exhibits a symmetric property that has remained consistently stable over extended periods, characterized by a symmetric distribution of package lengths with respect to mean length. We investigate the factors influencing this package flow distribution and reveal how network congestion protection mechanisms give rise to a exponential distribution. Our results demonstrate that the current packet emission behaviors in actual network infrastructure are dominated by these congestion control processes.

Although alkali plasma is a simple system, its thermodynamic properties are challenging to calculate due to complex correlations. The pair distribution function of monatomic systems, which describes system correlations, lacks a simple, precise analytical solution. A simple and precise formula for the pair distribution function of monatomic systems, which incorporates potential parameters, enables precise thermodynamic calculations for systems with known pair potentials. Moreover, this result provides an accurate model for comparing theoretical and experimental thermodynamic properties of alkali plasma in scientific literature, especially at high densities where d is significant, rendering simulations and classical approximations inaccurate.

Our investigation centers on how vector mesons' spectrum is affected by chiral asymmetry in the vacuum fermion density. By employing the in-medium spectral function approach, we analyze the roles of density-dependent self-energies for photons, rho, and omega mesons. As a starting point, we use the Thomas-Fermi approximation to derive the in-medium spectral functions, which reveal that the spectral functions of both rho and omega mesons exhibit low-energy peaks due to density effects. This phenomenon indicates that density influences the mass of these vector mesons, and notably, such a effect is more pronounced for the rho meson.

This research explores the challenge of estimating a large-scale network under conditions where some network nodes may be compromised and providing inaccurate information to the remaining nodes. Assuming that the network is small-world in nature, where most nodes are closely connected to a reference node through short paths, a cooperative algorithm is developed to estimate a network's scale despite the presence of malicious nodes. According to the theoretical findings, this algorithm produces an estimated scale that is not significantly overestimated with high confidence levels when the proportion of malicious nodes is less than 1/3rd, and the estimated scale is proportional to O(1/δ) when these conditions are met, where δ represents the maximum allowable error tolerable for estimation accuracy. A further analysis reveals that this estimated scale can be reduced to a value no greater than δ' when δ ≤ ρ and δ' ≤ ρ(1+ε) with ε being arbitrarily small and ρ being defined as β/(1-3β). It should also be noted that all estimates can be obtained by the healthy nodes in constant time after a single round of information exchange with their neighbors.

Our new method for creating initial data in numerical relativity involves creating two separate but balanced metric configurations representing an asymptotically flat spacetime at time zero. By adopting one of these metrics for our final choice, we determine the extrinsic curvature by analyzing how the metric's properties evolve from the metric's true representation. We then verify that this approach accurately accounts for both the scalar and momentum components of the initial data constraints. Initially, we applied the method to stationary and rotating black holes. Ultimately, our results indicate that this method can efficiently and precisely create complex data, particularly when dealing with multiple black holes.

JUNO will utilize approximately eight thousand twenty-inch PMTs, necessitating thorough quality assurance to minimize background events in future data analysis. To evaluate these PMTs, we employed various tests, including measuring mass screening parameters such as dark count rate, relative gain, and full width at half maximum using a P411 Phototest System and a 137Cs source. Our study investigates the impact of aging and temperature changes on the PMTs by analyzing dark counts obtained from the P411 and by suspending the PMTs in air at 50°C for forty days. The experiments revealed that the backplate and the B2001-30 dynode structure significantly influence the dark count of the PMTs. Our findings will serve as a foundation for developing improved age-dependent calibration methods, specifically the B2001-B2002 calibration, for the JUNO detector.

In our research, we developed an adaptive graph convolutional network (GCN) structure to predict time series data across multiple dimensions. This method combines node prediction, edge prediction, and an autoencoder that analyzes the differences between actual and compressed data to generate a model that accurately represents the characteristics of the data. By training an additional edge prediction module, our model can recover the graph structure, providing a clearer understanding of the data flow and enabling more accurate predictions. Contrary to existing GCN methods, which typically fix the graph structure, our adaptive approach creates a graph structure specific to the prediction task, allowing the model to explore new relationships between data points and producing more accurate predictions. Our model's effectiveness has been validated with real-world data and multiple custom datasets.

A comprehensive set of atmospheric dispersion measurements has been analyzed in detail. A notable discovery has been made - the Ca II h and K lines exhibit an unusual, significant excess of dispersion. This unusual excess has been accurately modeled for various wavelengths, and the resulting models have been created, which describe this excess across the visible spectrum. The resulting models have been compared with other on-sky measurements and other existing models in various test scenarios. Specifically, these new models have been shown to accurately predict the atmospheric dispersion of the VLT/UVES spectrograph and demonstrate a more precise estimation of the zero-point offset. Additionally, these new models have been demonstrated to provide accurate results for the estimation of the atmospheric dispersion of other instruments. A unique property of these new models is their ability to easily incorporate any new on-sky measurement by simply adjusting a universal zero-point offset.

In the realm of deep learning, knowledge distillation stands out as a prominent technique for enhancing model generalization by transferring explicit knowledge from a more sophisticated model to a less sophisticated one. Nevertheless, employing multiple instructors simultaneously poses challenges due to conflicting outputs, which can undermine the effectiveness of knowledge distillation. To tackle this issue, we introduce PILE, an approach that seamlessly integrates several instructor models by aggregating their pairwise logits comparisons. By establishing a unified framework for multi-instructor distillation, PILE ensures consistency across all instructor models by minimizing the sum of pairwise losses between them. Our study reveals that PILE outperforms existing distillation methods that consolidate knowledge through ensemble averaging and iterative aggregation of soft labels. Furthermore, the method produces results comparable to those of state-of-the-art approaches using a single instructor.

Bosonic shadow matter could take the form of super-cooled supermassive particles weighing between $10^{-6}$ and $10^{-3}$ eV. Researchers have developed detectors that utilize the Lorentz-violating properties predicted by certain theories to identify these particles through their effects on photon behavior. When such particles influence photons, they create refractive index variations over large distances, leading to changes in photon behavior. These variations occur at lengths of around micrometers to kilometers. As a result, these particles can induce correlations between photons regardless of their correlations or types. Consequently, detectors based on intensity interferometry, utilizing the Reiher-Feynman mechanism, are capable of detecting these particles without the need for single-photon sensitivity. Moreover, the development of such detectors can be expedited with the availability of off-the-shelf optics.

This paper explores the concept of uniqueness for solutions obtained through the Basis Pursuit approach, employing a continuous model formulated within the framework of subspaces in $\mathbb{R}^n$. We formulate specific criteria for determining the uniqueness of these solutions and illustrate their practical application via example. Additionally, our analysis reveals a substantial correspondence between the solutions of the continuous model and those of the traditional underdetermined linear system of equations, ultimately yielding a simplified characterization for uniqueness in the standard system.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model supporting compilers from multiple suppliers. Our open-source compiler for the P416 architecture builds on the ChipDIP framework to provide a reliable and adaptable compiler backend, featuring the first end-to-end compiler support for the P416 architecture and advanced optimizations including incremental evaluation and graph-based maclines optimization.

In numerical simulations involving moving boundaries using the Arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian approach, the vector transport equation arises. The accuracy of this transport process suffers when employing the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements due to the incorporation of logarithmic terms necessitated by the mesh quality assessment. We investigate two techniques to mitigate this loss of precision within the context of the mesh movement equation solved using the same finite elements. The first approach employs a simplified mesh quality metric incorporating the sought-after solution, thereby eliminating logarithmic terms. The second approach involves a modified time discretisation of the linear system representing the mesh movement through a dual time-stepping method. Both strategies are tested on a linear elastic material under finite elasticity principles using the second-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements, yielding improved simulation outcomes.

Federated learning's decentralized training environment is ideally suited to uphold user privacy within ethical boundaries, particularly when working with sensitive data sets. However, issues of biased outcomes also arise in this context, particularly when these data sets contain inherent biases. Researchers have investigated how federated learning's consensus mechanisms impact model fairness and efficiency in heterogeneous settings, particularly using methods such as FedAvg and its communication-efficient counterpart, FedProx. Experimental results indicate that Federated learning exacerbates model bias when multiple clients participate, compelling users to balance accuracy with fair representation. However, it has been found that utilizing the FedProx method in model training can mitigate this model bias, albeit potentially leading to a slight decline in communication efficiency.

Using (pb)(pb)→(pb)(bc+) collisions at a LHCb momentum of 2.032 TeV, we discovered the excited Bc+ state, denoted as 3SJ. We detected this state via its decay into J/ψ mesons and charged kaons, using the J/ψ mesons produced in pb collisions with nuclear targets and identified through their dimuon mode. Our experiments were conducted with significances of 6.1σ, yielding a total of 13 events, with a central resonance mass of 6806 MeV and a statistical precision of 51 MeV.

A new family of continuous-stage Runge-Kutta estimators is proposed to estimate and analyze the intermediate solution values generated during each step of a fixed-order method. By embedding these estimators, we can obtain a continuous approximation of the true solution to an initial value problem for a differential equation over the entire time span, for which global and local rates of convergence are proven. Building on top of existing Runge-Kutta theory and matrix notation, we conduct an analysis of efficiency and accuracy for these estimators and identify specific families of methods with optimal convergence rates.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of applications. As model complexity continues to grow, particularly in areas like computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition, DNN models are now large enough to benefit from distributed training. Existing solutions primarily rely on model-parallelism, splitting the DNN model across computing devices. However, this approach is restricted by memory constraints of individual devices, preventing the training of even slightly larger models. In response, a novel technique called regional critic training (RCT) has been developed to overcome this limitation. RCT enables a single DNN model to be replicated across multiple devices, significantly increasing its memory capacity and allowing for the training of larger models on smaller devices. Each device in this setup manages its own computational operations independently, minimizing data exchange between devices and optimizing computational efficiency. Extensive testing of RCT has been conducted using CUDA and OpenMP architectures, yielding notable speedups of up to 2x over current solution approaches.

Researchers in chaotic scattering studies have primarily concentrated on open systems where trajectories escape quickly. Our investigation centers around a complex, three-dimensional open system featuring a dissipation system where most initial conditions result in non-chaotic behavior characterized by Wada basins of varying sizes that share boundary points, forming a continuum from infinite to zero length. Contrary to expectations, relaxing the system's constraints results in faster trajectory escape times and enhanced mixing within the chaotic system, leading to improved practical applications of chaos-based processes.

We investigate hypothetical long-lived particles that are produced when heavier flavors transform into lighter ones, specifically considering decays like $\mu \to e$ and $\tau \to \mu$. These particles, denoted as $X$, have a particularly interesting property where their production from more massive flavors is unexpectedly enhanced compared to lighter flavors by a factor of $(m_T/m_X)^2$. This characteristic leads to unique consequences, specifically that while flavor-changing processes involving heavier flavors evade detection limits from high-precision tests, the decay of $X$ is instead constrained by a delayed appearance of electrons and muons following collisions in particle accelerators and by searches for neutron-related processes. This concept is specifically applicable to $Z'$ bosons, which connect lepton generations, and their existence could be probed through the use of the $10^{-14}$ sensitivity of upcoming muon-antimuon scattering experiments.

Human activity recognition in complex videos presents significant challenges, particularly due to diverse camera perspectives, complex activity structures, and variations in scale. Current approaches, which often struggle with real-world video datasets, rely on hand-crafted descriptors, and fail to account for the dependencies between scene and object, as well as temporal relationships. In this research, a novel Hierarchical Attention Network is proposed to automatically learn the most relevant features from raw image frames and focus on the most informative temporal segments, thus efficiently modeling the dependencies between scene and object, and temporal relationships. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks demonstrate the proposed method outperforms the current top-performing approaches, and it also proves to be robust and efficient for deployment on embedded devices.

This research explored recent developments in black hole thermodynamics and verified certain assumptions. We investigated a specific type of black hole, the Reissner-Nordstr$\ddot{o}$mn anti-de Sitter black hole with scalar field, in four dimensions, and obtained its thermodynamic properties and the temperature of the horizon. We verified the first law of black hole thermodynamics and found that it matches a known result, providing further confirmation of its validity. Additionally, we obtained the entropy of this black hole and confirmed that it is consistent with the area theorem. We also verified two hypotheses: the generalized second law of thermodynamics for this black hole and the feeble version of the cosmic censorship conjecture. Our study showed that the feeble version of the cosmic censorship conjecture can be violated under specific conditions, namely when the charge to mass ratio exceeds $\sqrt{2}$ in the presence of scalar field, leading to the complete collapse of the black hole and exposing its singularity. Furthermore, we found that this violation becomes even more pronounced as the self-coupling constant of the scalar field decreases. Our results reveal interesting thermodynamic properties and provide further confirmation of the feeble version of the cosmic censorship conjecture in the presence of scalar field, demonstrating that it can be violated under a broader range of conditions compared to the case without scalar field.

This paper explores the metaphorical significance of starlight and explores the scientific phenomenon of star formation, focusing on the conditions under which stars are born and how they illuminate the cosmos.

Using the Nested Sampling method, we have derived formulas for various entropy concepts based on the sampling density $p(\chi)$ in the parameter space with $d$ dimensions and $N$ points. As point count increases significantly, these entropies converge to values dependent only on that density. We offer a fresh perspective on maximum entropy methods and prove its equivalence to a constrained maximization approach. Entropy measures for both continuous and discrete variables are defined, as well as the mutual information between these variables. Our framework also includes a new expression for model evidence, and we verify these results through practical applications such as 2D Gaussian data and 3Spect data analysis.

We introduce a novel class of measure-valued solutions for nonlinear hyperbolic conservation laws, taking into account the oscillatory behavior of initial data within a small interval. This framework incorporates a initial probability measure that captures the data's long-term average, and it relies on particle trajectories derived from a related Hamilton-Jacobi equation. Although developed in one spatial dimension with a vector conservation law, our framework can be extended to general cases. It exhibits robustness against minor changes in data and provides insight into the formation of singularities by analyzing the evolution of collision sets in order to predict shock formation. Furthermore, our framework yields precise asymptotic profiles of solutions as their oscillation increases without bound, thus offering a link between oscillatory and faired-up initial data even in the presence of a faired-up profile change.

The proliferation of IoT devices has caused a significant expansion of attack surfaces due to their widespread adoption, particularly as many devices have inadequate protection against cyber threats. The influx of attacks has placed considerable demands on the performance of detection systems, chiefly due to the memory and processing capabilities required, which pose significant challenges especially for devices with resource constraints. In an effort to address this issue, this research paper proposes NBcoded, an innovative attack classification system that utilizes a codebook technique based on a least square encoder model coupled with Naive Bayes probability theory. NBcoded's efficiency has been verified through simulation and it has been found to optimize the requirements for memory and processing power by exploiting its compact nature. The simulated results showcased NBcoded's comparable performance in accuracy to existing detection systems while successfully adapting to devices with resource limitations.

Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with a generating set $S$. To measure how quickly elements of $G$ grow, we look at functions $f_G: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that satisfy certain conditions related to the size of balls in $G$. For groups where every element can be expressed using at most $k$ powers of generators from $S$, we establish lower and upper bounds for this growth rate in terms of $k$. To show that these bounds are meaningful across different groups, we provide an infinite family of solvable groups that have relatively slow growth rates.

Epidemiologists rely heavily on pinpointing rapid biological movements, such as virus and cell movement, to Biorad trackers. To supplement these results, our team developed an advanced computational framework for analyzing video recordings of biological motion. By leveraging cutting-edge neural network technology, the system automatically identifies key movement patterns, eliminating the need for extensive image pre-treatment. In our experiments with over 900 biorad recordings, our system achieved remarkable results in pinpointing rapid biological movement with high accuracy, closely matching the expertise of experienced researchers.

Optimizing power grid operations is crucial for maximizing efficiency and sustainability.
Optimizer tools are employed for various tasks, such as regulating electricity flow and
cost minimization during off-peak hours. We introduce a quantum algorithm that utilizes the QASM-Bench framework
to identify optimal solutions for operations-based power grid problems. Our results show that the quantum solution
aligns perfectly with the traditional computing solution but demands significant computational time for verification.
Key contributions of this paper are: employing quantum computation principles to enhance power grid operations; developing a QASM code to simulate quantum solutions; and obtaining realistic data from Power Systems Toolbox for validating our approach.

In search for a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental laws governing nature, machine learning models are emerging as a promising tool, leveraging data-driven and hypothesis-driven methodologies to identify consistent patterns in universal principles, conservation mechanisms, and energy functions, often uncovering discrepancies, noise, and complexities in real-world datasets, including cases where multiple explanations are plausible, thus requiring the development of systematic validation protocols.

This study investigates the presence of heavy particles for masses ranging from 150 to 3500 GeV that persist for extended periods before decaying within the detector's central area. The search is carried out using data collected by the ATLAS detector at the LHC in 2012, totaling 136 fb^-1 of data. The analysis focuses on the energy loss patterns of particles that are sensitive to the framework they traverse. The cut-based and multivariate techniques utilized in this research target high-mass particles with significant lifetimes and substantial energy losses. The results adhere to 95% confidence levels for cross-particle comparisons outlined in the theoretical models considered.

We have developed an integrated single-photon source utilizing quantum dot ridge waveguides, achieving high photon output efficiency in low-loss near-irradiance bands. By combining efficient light collection with defect-free quantum dots, our sources达近 unity efficacy, surpassing traditional approaches. Moreover, our sources exhibit narrow spectral widths and high degrees of purity. Specifically, we used indium arsenide quantum dots due to their high emission efficiency and narrow spectral widths. Designing optimized ridge waveguides via numerical methods enabled precise control of emission patterns. Our experiments demonstrated high performance across multiple wavelengths, including an external efficacy of 0.902 ± 0.026 for an emitting at 916 nanometers and external efficacy of 0.939 ± 0.020 for an emitting at 924 nanometers. Additionally, our achievement represents the highest purity at 276 nanoseconds.

In this research, our focus lies on achieving precise measurements of low-temperature specific heat and sound velocity for two types of materials: a precisely engineered glass, made of $\mathrm{Ge_2Sb_3Te_4}$, and various multilayered materials consisting of amorphous $\mathrm{Ge_2Sb_2O_6}$ layers, varied in thickness. Through these experiments, multiple indicators of a characteristic feature known as the boson peak were detected. Notably, the glass $\mathrm{Ge_2Sb_3Te_4}$ exhibited exceptional properties. These findings were confirmed using multiple techniques, including dynamic mechanical analysis, muon spin relaxation, and recent findings from light scattering and Raman studies. We utilized exact numerical calculations in our study as a tool to elucidate the nature of vibrational modes in these systems and their relationship to structural properties. Our results support the hypothesis that these vibrational modes originate from localized movements within molecular units, a type of building block found both in ideal and real glasses, whose influence can be isolated using sound velocity measurements and sound speed experiments.

The calculation of high-precision corrections in Quantum Field Theory is a crucial area of study that has seen significant advancements due to the capabilities of modern computer algebra systems. These systems have enabled the evaluation of complex multi-loop integrals through a variety of techniques, leading to precise predictions for theoretical predictions and addressing precise experimental findings. The resulting expressions are typically described using novel transcendental functions unlike many standard special functions commonly used before, prompting an examination of their properties and the potential applications in future predictions.

In diverse and intricate multidimensional scattering systems, we investigate the behavior of outgoing waves as a function of incoming wave parameters. Our focus lies on the relationship between this function when the incoming wave passes through an energy deposition eigenchannel, revealing that it behaves similarly to the system's overall size. Employing a one-dimensional model as a foundation, we demonstrate that this relationship arises from a unique sum rule that modifies the system's eigenwave expansion, potentially offering a unique method to analyze complex systems, particularly in terms of its topological properties.

Using archival data from various sources, a novel spiral arm structure in the galaxy has been uncovered, approximately 8-9 kiloparsecs away from the center, characterized by higher redshifts than expected. This discovery supports theories suggesting that the Galaxy's secondary spiral arms originate from the outer regions of the galaxy and support theories predicting the existence of a massive halo molecular cloud. Additionally, a significant movement of outer galaxy gas relative to the HII regions within this new arm has been identified.

Researchers interested in the diversity of solutions found during the optimization process, rather than just their quality, have been exploring this topic for some time. In response, a novel framework was developed to measure and analyze phenotype diversity in optimization algorithms. This framework facilitates a range of comparisons across different algorithms and encodings, and was utilized to investigate the characteristics of an optimization method known as Memetic Evolution, employing both real and binary encodings. Additionally, the influence of various parameters on algorithmic behavior was evaluated, leading to the creation of a variety of strategies for maintaining diverse outcomes in optimization processes.

A three-dimensional stable roommates problem was solved by designing an efficient algorithm that calculates three distinct preference lists for three different sets of entities - resources, male entities, and female entities. These lists represent additively separable preferences, where each entity's total satisfaction is determined by summing the satisfaction levels of individual resources. To account for asymmetry, each entity can have distinct preferences towards males and females and different levels of satisfaction from distinct resources. The problem's input includes three separate satisfaction tables, each detailing how much each entity is satisfied with a specific resource. The output consists of three distinct lists of preferred third parties for each set of entities - resources, males, and females. The runtime for solving this problem is O(n^2).

This study delves into valley dynamics within two-dimensional materials influenced by electron-phonon interactions. We've investigated how conventional phonon mechanisms and an unconventional mechanism where electrons create rigid shifts in atoms affect valley states within the framework of a Hamiltonian model. Our computations indicate that novel and conventional electron-phonon couplings have contrasting impacts on valley physics within this class of materials. While phonon interactions tend to broaden valley carriers, the unconventional mechanism actually enhances their lifespan. Moreover, we demonstrate that valley physics is highly sensitive to details of the electron-phonon interaction, specifically which atoms move and in what way. This sensitivity presents potential opportunities for tuning properties through novel electron-phonon interactions for applications in phononics and spinronics.

A cloud is defined as a dense subset in a metric space with the property that for any two space parameters, there exists a subset whose image under mapping to these spaces is dense in them. It's proven that any complete metric space contains a complete subset that satisfies this definition, thereby making the collection of Gromov-Hausdorff distances between these spaces metric. Similarly, any complete metric space has a subset that satisfies the definition of a cloud with parameters related to the original space diameter, essentially serving as its center.

This paper investigates the efficacy of planar antennas in the mm-wave spectrum for IoT applications, specifically considering their simplicity in fabrication using materials like RF laminate and flexible substrates, which offer advantageous properties such as conformability and bendability. A novel design of a patch antenna, constructed with an RF laminate substrate, exhibits significant bandwidth and a wide range of applicable angles. Through various tests, including bending experiments, the antenna's performance remains robust when subjected to different levels of flexibility. Furthermore, this research promotes the concept of integrating flexible antennas into wearable IoT devices, thereby opening possibilities for innovative designs beyond traditional rigid setups.

Achieving large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation necessitates a reliable and efficient method to correct potential errors during quantum operations. We develop a reinforcement learning framework for fault-tolerant quantum computation, focusing on two critical aspects: fault identification and error handling. Our approach trains two agents, a neural network-based classifier and a policy agent, to accurately identify faults and execute corrective actions based on fault patterns. Experimental results show that our proposed method achieves superior performance compared to conventional error correction techniques, ultimately facilitating the realization of large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation.

Advancements in sensor technology have made possible the operation of complex setups comprising multiple devices, enabling the measurement of intricate parameters within highly entangled systems. Our research focuses on estimating the amount of quantum entanglement, specifically in networks consisting of two cavities. We examine how estimating metrological resources influenced by quantum correlations is affected in such setups. Our study reveals that all methods of quantum state estimation mentioned in literature can be implemented in multi-cavity systems, and that certain estimators achieve lower quantum limits for quantum Fisher information when dealing with entangled states. Furthermore, we discovered that utilizing states with inherent quantum correlations can enhance the precision of metrological measurements compared to using product states.

The PHENIX collaboration measured direct photon-hadron associations in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions at 200 GeV per nucleon-on-nucleon. Comparing data from Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions, they found hadrons within direct photon pairs in Au$+$Au were less abundant and more central, indicating that the nuclear matter interacted with the hadrons. Furthermore, comparing the nuclear modification factors of direct photon-hadron associations with net-charge multiplets helped separate the effects of the hard process and the path that the parton takes through the medium, revealing that the nuclear modification factor depends on the momentum ratio of the hadron to the direct photon, rather than the overall pair momentum.

In this research, we demonstrate the feasibility of emulating complex fermionic systems on a universal quantum computer without specialized hardware. Our method combines digital and analog techniques to efficiently represent complex Hamiltonians using a mixture of digital circuits and precomputed commutator terms. Its digital component achieves a significant reduction in digital quantum gates requirement, providing a crucial barrier against fermion-qubit ratio limitations. Its hybrid combination leads to a straightforward mapping of hybrid circuits to complex fermionic systems. Through simulation studies, we illustrate the practical implementation of our algorithm using the IBM quantum cloud platform for a choice of fermionic models, including the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model for one- and two-dimensional fermionic lattice systems. Our results also include digital-analog quantum circuits for one-dimensional systems up to 20 sites, enabling the rapid exploration of quantum advantage for multimodal fermionic simulations.

In financial trading, integrating features derived from past asset performance into predictive models is a crucial task. Traditionally, traders employ heuristic methods, such as technical indicators, to generate this information. However, this paper presents a data-driven approach, framing it as a conditional generadative task, to develop features. Our methodology leverages a non-parametric convolutional neural network, tailored to handle the inherent challenges in financial data, such as concept drift and conceptual ambiguity. Experimental results demonstrate that our method yields superior outcomes compared to traditional approaches, providing a viable solution to the longstanding dilemma in finance between model optimization and generalization.

Achieving the formation of intricate three-dimensional structures within the eyes of living organisms holds great potential for groundbreaking research in optogenetics and existing therapies like raster electrotransfer. However, controlling multi-FLC multi-phase SLM systems to deliver complex 3D energy patterns within tissue has been an unmet challenge. To overcome this obstacle, we have developed an innovative approach for generating complex three-dimensional structures within tissue, utilizing an iterative fluence correction technique to optimize a complex light field. Through extensive simulations and experiments involving bovine eye cornea tissue, we have successfully demonstrated our approach's capability to reproduce complex three-dimensional patterns, thereby paving the way for our system's application in optogenetics, raster electrotransfer, and photodynamic therapy.

We appreciate the discussion sparked by our initial publication. The discussion highlights four key aspects: (1) The need for sharper bounds on decision-making under uncertainty; (2) The potential to incorporate more complex decision-making rules; (3) The value of considering patient subgroups based on multiple characteristics; and (4. The desire for more efficient learning methods. In response, we discuss our agreement with the discussions on (1) and (3), offering some supplementary insights. However, we discuss potential challenges associated with the incorporation suggested in (2); and finally, we present several suggestions aimed at accelerating the learning process described in(3).

A prototype detector known as CLICTD is being developed as a technology demonstration for monolithic small-pixel detectors featuring segmentation on the collection electrode. Constructed using a high-resistivity silicon substrate, the active layer is made of p-on-n photodiode technology with a thickness of approximately 3-4 microns. By combining this with a large pixel size of around 800x800 microns, CLICTD aims to achieve high spatial resolution while maintaining low noise levels. The proposed detector will serve as a technology proof-of-concept and also as a versatile silicon sensor that can be utilized in various SiPM-based devices and modules. The project involves creating multiple detector types through experimental testing of different materials including high-resistivity silicon and compound semiconductor substrates such as GaAs and InP. The research involves measuring the electrical and optical properties of these materials and simulating their performance. The research results reveal that the chosen sensor parameters result in excellent timing, significant improvements in signal-to-noise ratio (up to 5 times greater than traditional designs), and enhanced energy efficiency. These results indicate that the CLICTD prototype has the potential for use in various applications including spectral imaging, small-angle x-ray scattering, and x-ray phase contrast imaging.

Advanced optical systems are significantly hindered by atmospheric turbulence, which is particularly severe at high altitudes, resulting in low-quality images with restricted resolution.  A novel technique called the Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent camera (FAST) has been proposed to mitigate this problem.  Recently, research institutions have established a functional prototype of FAST to conduct pioneering experiments.  We present here results from initial experiments using the prototype on a testbed at Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics (SCEAO) Lab.  By leveraging fast orbitally locked telescopes to target a stationary spacecraft, we demonstrated that FAST can effectively leverage residual atmospheric speckles to produce a compensated image.  Our novel approach involves controlling individual speckles in real-time using a high-performance adaptive optics system in a closed-loop configuration to directly translate low-order speckles into a targeted image.  Our experimental results show that FAST can produce images at a rate of 500 Hz with contrast improvements of up to four orders of magnitude through real-time wavefront correction.  We further examined FAST's performance limitations under various operating conditions, which reveal a potential 100% contrast recovery at 10 Hz.  We also investigated the implications of motion blur, which may limit the fastest imaging rates to approximately 50 Hz.  We compared the experimental findings with a theoretical model that accurately predicts the technique's capabilities.  Our research suggests that FAST can be integrated into existing adaptive optics systems to produce a new type of "super-secondary

This study presents a novel negative interest rate model inspired by the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross framework, incorporating the deterministic-shift feature utilized in the Leiden and Boerenwinst negative interest rate models. Thorough mathematical examinations are conducted to assess key model properties, and empirical analyses using in-sample and out-of-sample data are performed to evaluate the models. Specific statistical metrics, and trading strategies informed by switch points are developed to assess the models, ultimately revealing that the model under investigation outperforms both the Leiden and Boerenwinst models.

Meta-analytic studies often involve multiple unrelated groups of studies, and  analyzing 2xK structured data in such contexts (with two outcomes across various effects) can enhance understanding of treatment effects from existing research. However, current analysis methods are mainly restricted to univariate findings, which may overlook crucial information. Although some prior work attempted to address this gap, existing approaches often rely on strong assumptions regarding underlying data distributions or become computationally intensive. In our investigation, we explore key parameters from a meta-analytic model with k unrelated groups, focusing on cluster-robust variance estimation for primary effects, such as the average shift and contrast effects. These estimates remain valid regardless of the number of classes. We assessed their efficiency compared to efficient estimators, observed that they perform well when efficients estimators are biased due to issues like publication bias, and typically offer improved accuracy over alternative estimators. Furthermore, we derived asymptotically equivalent estimators, which can be useful in practical applications, and applied these methods to analyze the impact of antipsychotic medications on multiple measures of psychiatric symptoms.

Molecular dynamics simulations of particle-based systems can be made significantly more efficient through the use of time-decomposition strategies, especially when physical forces like Lennard-Jones interactions are involved, which act over a very short range and can be integrated on a much smaller time-step compared to soft forces like springs or Coulomb interactions. Although this approach is commonly applied to systems with hard-sphere collisions, its utility for models that account for finite collision times – such as the granular liquid described by the granular Langevin equation – has been largely overlooked. Through numerical experiments, we demonstrate that a time-decomposition approach can be successfully adapted for simulations with short-range attractive forces, yielding substantial speedups while maintaining simulation accuracy.

In this paper, we provide an in-depth explanation of the origin of radiative energy loss due to Unruh-Hawking effect and the corresponding increase in temperature of a black hole. We employ the concepts of negative energy and particle number conservation within the context of quantum field theory to address these questions. We initially explore the energy emission from an accelerating observer and a black hole from a quantum field's perspective, leveraging the concept of mode orthogonality. We demonstrate that radially outward-directed field disturbances with negative energy play a crucial role. We further investigate the energy balance in this process, confirming that the energy radiated away is compensated by the increase in the accelerator's kinetic energy. We then investigate the energy emission from a static black hole and a uniformly accelerating observer, further verifying our findings in a quantum field theory approach.

This study evaluates one- and two-jet event shapes at the LHC within the color dipole framework, notably investigating how Fadin-Kuraev-Lipatov resummation impacts negative-odd moment nucleon structure functions, such as $g_1^N$ and $g_2^N$. We examine the role of twist-1, twist-2, $g_1$-type twist-3, and $g_2$-type twist-3 parton distribution functions (PDFs) in shaping these shapes, particularly focusing on $x$-dependence influenced by twist-3 $g_1^T(x,Q^2)$ and twist-3 $h_1^T(x,Q^2, Q')$. Our analysis reveals that a conventional set of twist-3 $g_1^T(x,Q^2)$ and twist-3 $h_1^T(x,Q^2, Q')$ exhibits a distinct $Q^2$-dependence compared to their respective conventional twist-3 $f_2^T(x,Q^2)$ and twist-3 $f_1^T(x,Q^2)$ counterparts, suggesting these conventional distributions may be negligible or even anti-chiral-odd. We leverage existing literature on conventional twist-3 $f_2^T(x,Q^2)$ and twist-3 $f_1^T(x,Q^2)$ to constrain their corresponding $g_1^T

This article presents a proof that specific integer pairs raised to different powers form unique combinations with product-based pairs that satisfy the given equation for all positive integers n. It builds on a foundational problem solved by Delone and Baryakhtar in 1970, providing a novel proof with potential applications in similar mathematical contexts.

When a liquid jet from an adjustable nozzle merges with a flowing solvent in a channel and forms an ellipsoidal bubble, it creates unstable vibrations that manifest as a visible pattern known as a "danceing jet." This phenomenon results in the bubble taking on periodic structures along the stream's direction in the flow regime called Type-I. By analyzing the interface between the jet and the surrounding fluid as a nonlinear dynamic system, it is possible to predict specific characteristics, such as the distance between structures, their amplitude variations, and the wavelength of the undulations. The theoretical model demonstrates excellent agreement with observed experimental results.

As we increasingly rely on high-performance computing systems built on non-volatile memory, developing methods to recover data after a system crash becomes a pressing challenge.
